title: Greene v. McElroy (1959)
summary: Without explicit authorization from Congress or the President, the Defense Department could not revoke a defense contractor employee's security clearance, and so destroy his career, through hearings that denied him confrontation and cross examination of his accusers.
notes:
Key line: "Without explicit action by lawmakers, decisions of great constitutional import and effect would be relegated by default to administrators who, under our system of government, are not endowed with authority to decide them." (Warren, C.J.)

Citation: 360 U.S. 474 (1959).

sections.Parties: The petitioner was William L. Greene, an aeronautical engineer who had been vice president and general manager of Engineering and Research Corporation (ERCO), a private company in Riverdale, Maryland, that developed and manufactured mechanical and electronic products, much of it classified work for the armed services. The respondents were the Secretary of Defense, Neil McElroy, and the Secretaries of the Army, Navy and Air Force. Greene sued them for a declaration that the revocation of his security clearance was unlawful and void and for an order restraining them from acting under it. The American Civil Liberties Union filed a brief as amicus curiae urging reversal.
sections.Material Facts: Greene joined ERCO in 1937 after graduating from the Guggenheim School of Aeronautics and rose to chief executive officer. He held clearances granted in 1949 and 1950. On December 11, 1951, the Army Navy Air Force Personnel Security Board revoked his clearance on charges that between 1943 and 1947 he had associated with Communists, entertained Russian Embassy officers, and attended a Southern Conference for Human Welfare dinner. At a hearing on January 23, 1952, he testified with counsel and produced ERCO executives and military officers as witnesses; the government called no witnesses and relied on confidential reports he never saw. The Industrial Employment Review Board restored his clearance on January 29, 1952. After the program was reorganized in March 1953, the Secretary of the Navy wrote ERCO on April 17, 1953, without a hearing, that Greene's access was inconsistent with national security, and ERCO discharged him. His salary fell from $18,000 to $4,400.
sections.Procedural History: Greene sued in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia for a declaratory judgment that the revocation of his clearance was unlawful and for an injunction against the Secretaries. The district court granted summary judgment for the government. The Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit affirmed, 254 F.2d 944 (1958), holding that the procedures were authorized and did not violate the Constitution. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, heard argument on April 1, 1959, and on June 29, 1959, reversed and remanded to the district court for proceedings not inconsistent with its opinion.
sections.Issue: Whether the Department of Defense, acting under regulations promulgated by the Secretary of Defense without explicit authorization by either Congress or the President, could deprive a defense contractor's employee of his security clearance, and thereby of his job and his profession, in administrative proceedings in which he was denied access to much of the adverse information and any opportunity to confront and cross examine the witnesses against him. The Court also considered, but did not decide, whether such procedures would violate the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment if they were explicitly authorized.
sections.Holding: The Court held that in the absence of explicit authorization from either the President or Congress the Secretaries were not empowered to deprive Greene of his job in a proceeding in which he was not afforded the safeguards of confrontation and cross examination. Neither Executive Order 10290 nor Executive Order 10501 authorized such a program; the National Security Act of 1947 and the Armed Services Procurement Act, read with the espionage and classified information statutes, were not authorizations to create it; and continued appropriations did not ratify hearing procedures Congress was never told about. The Court expressly did not decide the constitutional question, whether the President had inherent authority, or what the limits of executive or legislative power might be.
sections.Reasoning: Chief Justice Warren traced the history of the industrial security program and found that it had been built by the Department of Defense on its own, with the President and Congress at most acquiescing. The government's own brief conceded the program was not explicitly authorized by statute. The Court explained that where administrative action raises serious constitutional problems, it assumes that Congress or the President intended to afford those affected the traditional safeguards of due process, citing the Japanese Immigrant Case, Ex parte Endo, Peters v. Hobby and Kent v. Dulles. Confrontation and cross examination have long been thought essential when governmental action seriously injures an individual and the reasonableness of the action depends on findings of fact, especially where the evidence consists of statements by faceless informers whose reliability cannot be tested. Acquiescence or implied ratification would suffice to show delegation in areas where the government's freedom to act is clear, and the Court had no difficulty finding authority for a clearance program that afforded confrontation and cross examination. But decisions of great constitutional import must be made explicitly by those responsible for enacting and implementing the laws, so that careful and purposeful consideration is assured, and cannot be relegated by default to administrators. Because the procedures used against Greene had never been explicitly authorized, the revocation could not stand.

topics.lrs-o-new-property: Severe impairment of occupational opportunity mattered even though the reported holding rested on lack of delegated authority for the procedure.

learning.separateOpinions: The judgment was 8 to 1. Justices Frankfurter, Harlan and Whittaker concurred in the judgment on the ground that neither Congress nor the President had authorized the procedures, expressing no view on their validity. Justice Harlan also wrote separately to say that the Court's opinion unnecessarily dealt with the very constitutional issue it disclaimed deciding, and that the courts should not decide the constitutionality of nonconfrontation procedures until Congress or the President has deliberately considered and expressly authorized them. Justice Clark dissented, calling the case clear and simple: no one has a constitutional right of access to the government's military secrets, and the Cabinet members had merely refused Greene further access after a series of hearings.
